annotations.text:
Dossier direction, developed. All three artboards are live — click into them.

Entry: five fields, including the optional Hebrew name. Its hint is live — leave it blank and it explains that the Latin name gets transliterated and that Kabbalah lowers its own confidence rather than pretending. Every field says which systems it feeds.

Profile: nine dimensions, 32 traits. Click any row to open its facets and see who said what. Tick "I don't know my birth time" first, and watch two systems step back while the counts fall from six to four.

BREADTH — what the first pass got wrong.

It showed three traits from one dimension, which undersold the engine badly. The real taxonomy is 32 traits across nine dimensions, and six of those nine carry four facets rather than three. I read that out of kb/facets.yaml rather than from memory the second time, which is how the error got in.

The problem breadth creates is nine strong-sounding claims flattening into noise. One editorial rule holds it together: the hero claim above the list is the single most-agreed trait in the whole profile, and it says so — "nothing else below is backed by more." Everything under it is then read relative to that.

ALL 32 AT ONCE.

The nine-dimension list gives prose one dimension at a time; this gives the whole shape in one screen. Every dot is one tradition on the side it argued for, so agreement reads as a cluster and disagreement reads as a straddle — no number to parse.

Two colour decisions, both settled by running the validator rather than by eye. A second mark colour for majority-versus-minority FAILED the normal-vision separation floor against the terracotta (ΔE 13.9, below 15) — and chasing a passing pair surfaced that the idea was wrong anyway: rendering a minority reading in pale grey visually discounts it, which is the opposite of what this engine claims to do. Every dot now weighs the same and position does all the work.

The two evenly-split rows are tinted with a marked centre. Rows where only two traditions spoke are tagged "thin", so sparse evidence does not read as confidently as dense evidence. Hover any row for who said what.

TRAIT BY TRAIT.

The three scores at the top are what the compatibility endpoint actually returns — connection, communication, growth. The section below is the playground doing something the endpoint does not: laying both stored profiles side by side across all 32 traits.

Filled dot is you, open ring is Theo. Same side means you will not have to negotiate it; opposite sides are tinted, because those are the ones worth knowing early. Two rows read "you are split" — the six could not agree about you there, so there is nothing to compare, and the design says so rather than inventing a side.

Shape rather than a second colour, deliberately: it needs no colour pair to validate, and it survives colour-blindness and greyscale printing.

Open question: whether the viewer is always one of the two ("You and Theo") or two arbitrary people can be compared. The API allows either; second person is warmer, third is more honest when neither chart is yours.

Kept for reference. B was chosen; A — Instrument has been retired from the canvas.

If any of C's show-your-working density or D's restraint is worth folding in later, it is easier to argue from these than from memory.
